name: Malyavanta Raghunatha Temple, Hampi
deity: Rama as Raghunatha, with Sita, Lakshmana and a kneeling Hanuman, carved on the great boulder that forms the sanctum
period: A hilltop shrine of the Vijayanagara capital, endowed by 1559 CE under Sadashiva Raya; still in worship
style: Dravidian, Vijayanagara phase, built around a natural boulder
summary: On Malyavanta hill, which tradition holds is where Rama and Lakshmana waited out the monsoon before the search for Sita, a living Vijayanagara temple rises around a giant boulder carved with Rama's family.

sections.history: Malyavanta hill rises on the eastern edge of the old Vijayanagara city, above what was once its urban core, and its temple to Rama as Raghunatha has drawn worshippers since imperial times. An inscription dated Saka 1481, or 1559 CE, in the reign of Sadashiva Raya, records a grant of land to the god, named in it as Malyavanta-Raghunathadeva, to maintain a charitable water trough — evidence that the shrine was already established and endowed in the last years of the empire. When the capital fell in 1565, worship here was not extinguished, and the temple remains a living shrine amid the ruins of the World Heritage site of Hampi.
sections.architecture: The temple is built around a massive granite boulder, and the sanctum is the rock itself: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana, with Hanuman kneeling before them, are carved on its face. The boulder rises clean through the roof of the shrine, and a small built tower has been set upon its summit, so that nature and the builders together supply the vimana. The walled complex is entered through two gopurams in the Vijayanagara manner, a five-storeyed tower on the south and a three-storeyed one on the east, and holds a goddess shrine and a small Shiva shrine. Nearby, a cleft in the rock is carved with rows of lingas and Nandis.
sections.legends: Tradition identifies Malyavanta with Mount Prasravana of the Ramayana. After Sugriva was crowned king of Kishkindha, the rains set in and the search for Sita had to wait; Rama and Lakshmana spent the four months of the monsoon sheltering on this hill, Rama grieving for Sita while Lakshmana kept watch and urged him to hope. When the rains ended, the monkey armies gathered and the search began that would lead to Lanka. Devotees climb the hill to stand where, as the story holds, Rama waited and prayed.
sections.festivals: As a living Rama temple, Malyavanta Raghunatha keeps the Vaishnava calendar, with Rama Navami as its chief festival; Hanuman Jayanti, honouring the devotee who kneels in the carving, is customarily marked as well, and bhajan singing is a regular part of worship here. Confirm dates and any special observances locally.
sections.experience: A road winds up to the hilltop, and the view repays the climb: the boulder country of Hampi spreads in every direction, with the Tungabhadra glinting to the north. The hill is a favourite place to watch the sunset. Enter through the southern gopuram, stand before the carved boulder in the cool of the sanctum, then walk around the outside to see the rock rising through the roof.

visit.timings: A living temple, generally open from morning to evening with a midday break; confirm timings locally.
visit.dressCode: Modest dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed before entering the shrine.
visit.photography: Photography of the complex and the hilltop views is generally fine; follow the priests' guidance about the sanctum.
visit.gettingThere: Malyavanta hill lies on the east side of the Hampi ruins, south-east of the Vittala temple and a few kilometres by road from Hampi Bazaar and Kamalapura, with a road to the top. Hampi lies in Vijayanagara district, Karnataka; Hosapete (Hospet), about 13 km away, has the nearest railway station, and Bengaluru is roughly 340 km by road.
